Her respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute and she was hypotensive. An arterial blood gas indicated a type 1 respiratory failure (Pa02 7.2 kPa and PaC02 4.0 kPa). Her Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) was seven (withdrawing and opening eyes to pain, without a verbal response). She was transferred to intensive care for intubation and ventilation the day after admission.

report.source_text: At day ten postextubation, she underwent an EEG. Frequent (2.5–4 Hz), florid bilateral, non-synchronous epileptiform discharges were seen over both hemispheres throughout most of the recording. The patient was unresponsive during this period of recording. 2mg of intravenous lorazepam was given, after which the epileptiform discharges subsided and a 6–7 Hz background predominated. The patient became slightly more alert, in that she could obey some motor commands and vocalise to a small extent.

Two days later she was less engaged, she was unable to speak or obey commands and opened her eyes only to pain. Some new onset intermittent right-sided facial jerks were noted. She was diagnosed with NCSE on electroencephalogram (EEG). She was commenced on Levetiracetam.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 57-year-old woman presented with shortness of breath and fever, found to be lethargic with a GCS of 7 and type 1 respiratory failure, requiring intubation and ventilation. After approximately one month of intubation, and two days after achieving a GCS of 15 and self-ventilating (around May 27th), she experienced neurological deterioration with decreased engagement, inability to speak or obey commands, and new onset intermittent right-sided facial jerks. An EEG performed around day ten post-extubation (approximately June 4th) showed frequent (2.5–4 Hz), florid bilateral, non-synchronous epileptiform discharges, confirming Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus (NCSE). These discharges subsided with intravenous lorazepam, leading to improved alertness. A follow-up EEG the next day showed persistent multifocal epileptiform discharges. She was commenced on Levetiracetam, leading to gradual improvement in verbalization and motor commands, though she experienced fluctuating confusion three weeks after discharge to the neurology ward, attributed to a concomitant urinary tract infection.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with severe respiratory distress and altered mental status, requiring intubation.
Neurological deterioration occurred with new onset intermittent right-sided facial jerks and decreased responsiveness around May 27th, after extubation.
First EEG (day ten post-extubation) showed frequent, florid bilateral, non-synchronous epileptiform discharges, confirming NCSE.
Epileptiform discharges subsided and alertness improved after 2mg intravenous lorazepam.
A second EEG one day later showed persistent multifocal epileptiform discharges.
Patient gradually improved, able to verbalize and obey motor commands, though later experienced fluctuating confusion with a UTI.

remaining_uncertainties: Initial brain imaging and other lab tests to rule out alternative causes of altered mental status were not documented.
